steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on making causal attribution of LLM behaviour to model components cheaper and more scalable, using Attribution Patching and an improved variant. Motivate the problem, describe the cost of existing methods, explain our approach, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Mechanistic interpretability and causal attribution to components
- Ablation and Activation Patching
- Cost of sweeping all components in large models
- Our approach: AtP as a prefilter plus verification
- Contributions (AtP*, baselines, systematic study, diagnostic)
- Practical guidance

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - LLMs ubiquitous, integrated into many digital applications
  - understanding internal mechanisms = mechanistic interpretability
  - subproblem: causally attribute behaviours to parts of the transformer forward pass (attention heads, neurons, layer contributions, residual streams), often at specific token positions
  - complex behaviours driven by sparse subgraphs (cite)
- Methods
  - zero-ablation / knock-out: delete component, see if output gets worse -> causally important
  - generalised: replace activations with samples from a baseline distribution (zero-ablation special case)
  - focus: Activation Patching, aka causal mediation analysis (cite); baseline = activations on corrupted input, e.g. alternate string with different answer (cite)
- Cost
  - common to sweep all components, intervening on each via resampling (cite)
  - SoTA models: expensive for small components (heads, neurons); one forward pass per intervention -> millions or billions
  - prompt length 1024: 2.7\cdot 10^{9} neuron nodes in Chinchilla 70B (cite)
- Approach
  - Attribution Patching (AtP) (cite): faster, approximate causal attribution, used as prefilter
  - iterate nodes in decreasing |AtP estimate|, verify with Activation Patching, filter false positives = verification
  - only care about small set of top nodes -> verification far cheaper than all nodes
- Contributions
  - AtP performance study: two failure modes giving false negatives -> AtP*
    - queries/keys: recompute attention softmax, then gradient approximation (gradients poor for saturated attention)
    - dropout on backwards pass for brittle false negatives (positive and negative effects cancel)
  - alternative methods approximating Activation Patching as baselines, beat brute force
  - first systematic study: AtP beats all others, AtP* further improvement
  - diagnostic: filter high impact nodes with AtP, patch random subsets of remainder -> bound remaining false negatives
- Guidance in Section 5.4 on practical causal attribution

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
LLMs are becoming ubiquitous and are integrated into many digital applications, so understanding the internal mechanisms behind their behaviour is an increasingly pressing research problem – this is the problem of mechanistic interpretability. A basic subproblem is to causally attribute particular behaviours to individual parts of the transformer forward pass, which correspond to specific components (like attention heads, neurons, layer contributions, or residual streams), often at specific positions in the input token sequence. This matters because in many case studies of complex behaviours, the behaviours are found to be driven by sparse subgraphs within the model.

A classic form of causal attribution is zero-ablation, or knock-out, where a component is deleted and we see if this makes the model's output worse – if it does, the component was causally important. More recent work has generalised this to replacing a component's activations with samples from some baseline distribution (zero-ablation is the special case where activations are resampled to be zero). We focus on Activation Patching (also known as causal mediation analysis), which is popular and widely used. Here the baseline distribution is a component's activations on some corrupted input, such as an alternate string with a different answer.

Once you have a causal attribution method, it is common to sweep across all model components and directly evaluate the effect of intervening on each of them via resampling. But with SoTA models it can be expensive to attribute behaviour, especially to small components (e.g. heads or neurons) – every intervention needs a separate forward pass, so the number of forward passes can easily go into the millions or billions. For example, on a prompt of length 1024, Chinchilla 70B has 2.7\cdot 10^{9} neuron nodes.

- Approach
  - Attribution Patching (AtP): faster, approximate causal attribution, used as prefilter
  - go through nodes in decreasing |AtP estimate|, Activation Patching to filter false positives = verification
  - small set of top nodes -> verification much cheaper than all nodes
- Contributions
  - AtP failure modes (false negatives) -> AtP*:
    - queries/keys: recompute attention softmax, then gradient approximation (saturated attention)
    - dropout on backwards pass for brittle false negatives (effects cancel)
  - alternative baselines approximating Activation Patching, beat brute force
  - first systematic study: AtP best, AtP* further improvement
  - diagnostic: AtP filters high impact nodes, patch random subsets of the rest; bound remaining false negatives
- Section 5.4: practical guidance on causal attribution

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
LLMs are becoming ubiquitous and are integrated into many digital applications, so understanding the internal mechanisms behind their behaviour is an increasingly pressing research problem – this is the problem of mechanistic interpretability. A basic subproblem is to causally attribute particular behaviours to individual parts of the transformer forward pass, which correspond to specific components (like attention heads, neurons, layer contributions, or residual streams), often at specific positions in the input token sequence. This matters because in many case studies of complex behaviours, the behaviours are found to be driven by sparse subgraphs within the model.

A classic form of causal attribution is zero-ablation, or knock-out, where a component is deleted and we see if this makes the model's output worse – if it does, the component was causally important. More recent work has generalised this to replacing a component's activations with samples from some baseline distribution (zero-ablation is the special case where activations are resampled to be zero). We focus on Activation Patching (also known as causal mediation analysis), which is popular and widely used. Here the baseline distribution is a component's activations on some corrupted input, such as an alternate string with a different answer.

Once you have a causal attribution method, it is common to sweep across all model components and directly evaluate the effect of intervening on each of them via resampling. But with SoTA models it can be expensive to attribute behaviour, especially to small components (e.g. heads or neurons) – every intervention needs a separate forward pass, so the number of forward passes can easily go into the millions or billions. For example, on a prompt of length 1024, Chinchilla 70B has 2.7\cdot 10^{9} neuron nodes.

We propose to speed this process up by using Attribution Patching (AtP), which is a faster, approximate causal attribution method, as a prefiltering step. After running AtP, we go through the nodes in decreasing order of the absolute value of the AtP estimate, and then use Activation Patching to evaluate these nodes more reliably and filter out false positives – we call this verification. Usually we care about a small set of top contributing nodes, so verification is much cheaper than going over all nodes.

- We look into the performance of AtP and find two classes of failure modes that produce false negatives. We propose a variant of AtP called AtP ∗, which makes two changes to address these failure modes while keeping scalability:

- – When patching queries and keys, recomputing the attention softmax and using a gradient based approximation after that, since gradients are a poor approximation to saturated attention.

- – Using dropout on the backwards pass to fix brittle false negatives, where significant positive and negative effects cancel out.

- We introduce several alternative methods that approximate Activation Patching, as baselines to AtP, and they outperform brute force Activation Patching.

- We present the first systematic study of AtP and these alternatives, and we show that AtP significantly outperforms all the other methods we investigated, and AtP ∗ gives a further significant improvement.

- To estimate the residual error of AtP ∗ and statistically bound the sizes of any false negatives that remain, we provide a diagnostic method. It is based on using AtP to filter out high impact nodes and then patching random subsets of the rest. With good diagnostics, practitioners can still gauge whether AtP is reliable in the domains they care about without paying for exhaustive verification.

Finally, in Section 5.4 we give some guidance on how to do causal attribution successfully in practice, and which attribution methods are likely to be useful and when.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
As LLMs become ubiquitous and integrated into numerous digital applications, understanding the internal mechanisms that underlie their behaviour is an increasingly pressing research problem – this is the problem of mechanistic interpretability. A fundamental subproblem is to causally attribute particular behaviours to individual parts of the transformer forward pass, corresponding to specific components (such as attention heads, neurons, layer contributions, or residual streams), often at specific positions in the input token sequence. This is important because in numerous case studies of complex behaviours, they are found to be driven by sparse subgraphs within the model [1,2,3].

A classic form of causal attribution uses zero-ablation, or knock-out, where a component is deleted and we see whether this negatively affects the model’s output – a negative effect implies the component was causally important. More recent work has generalised this to replacing a component’s activations with samples from some baseline distribution (zero-ablation being the special case where activations are resampled to be zero). We focus on the popular and widely used method of Activation Patching (also known as causal mediation analysis) [4,3,5], where the baseline distribution is a component’s activations on some corrupted input, such as an alternate string with a different answer [6,7].

Given a causal attribution method, it is common to sweep across all model components, directly evaluating the effect of intervening on each of them via resampling [3]. However, with SoTA models it can be expensive to attribute behaviour, especially to small components (e.g. heads or neurons) – each intervention requires a separate forward pass, so the number of forward passes can easily climb into the millions or billions. For example, on a prompt of length 1024, there are 2.7\cdot 10^{9} neuron nodes in Chinchilla 70B [8].

We propose to accelerate this process by using Attribution Patching (AtP) [9], a faster, approximate causal attribution method, as a prefiltering step: after running AtP, we iterate through the nodes in decreasing order of the absolute value of the AtP estimate, then use Activation Patching to evaluate these nodes more reliably and filter out false positives – we call this verification. Since we typically care about a small set of top contributing nodes, verification is far cheaper than iterating over all nodes.

- We investigate the performance of AtP, finding two classes of failure modes which produce false negatives. We propose a variant of AtP called AtP ∗, with two changes that address these failure modes while retaining scalability:

- – When patching queries and keys, recomputing the attention softmax and using a gradient based approximation from then on, as gradients are a poor approximation to saturated attention.

- – Using dropout on the backwards pass to fix brittle false negatives, where significant positive and negative effects cancel out.

- We introduce several alternative methods to approximate Activation Patching as baselines to AtP, which outperform brute force Activation Patching.

- We present the first systematic study of AtP and these alternatives and show that AtP significantly outperforms all other investigated methods, with AtP ∗ providing a further significant improvement.

- To estimate the residual error of AtP ∗ and statistically bound the sizes of any remaining false negatives, we provide a diagnostic method based on using AtP to filter out high impact nodes and then patching random subsets of the remainder. Good diagnostics mean that practitioners can still gauge whether AtP is reliable in relevant domains without the costs of exhaustive verification.

Finally, we provide some guidance in Section 5.4 on how to perform causal attribution successfully in practice, and on which attribution methods are likely to be useful under which circumstances.
